subject: Electromagnetic Theory
scope: A CSIR-NET focused treatment of Maxwell's equations from physical motivation and four laws through differential and integral forms, boundary conditions, electromagnetic waves, Poynting theorem, worked problems, traps and revision.
learning_outcomes: State and interpret all four Maxwell equations in integral and differential form.
Convert correctly between flux/circulation integrals and local differential equations using Gauss and Stokes theorems.
Explain displacement current and why Ampere's law must be completed for time-dependent fields.
Derive the electromagnetic wave equation and identify wave speed, impedance and transverse polarization.
Apply Maxwell boundary conditions and use them in standard CSIR-NET interface problems.
Use the Poynting vector and Poynting theorem to analyze electromagnetic energy transport and power flow.
Recognize symmetry, sign, orientation, limiting-case and dimensional traps in Part B/C questions.

historical_journey.story: Gauss, Faraday and Ampere supplied complementary laws for electric charge, magnetic fields and induction, but the laws were not yet a complete dynamical field theory.
Maxwell introduced the displacement-current term, making charge conservation compatible with the field equations and predicting self-sustaining electromagnetic waves.
The four equations are local conservation/field relations that unify electrostatics, magnetostatics, induction, radiation and energy transport.

why_this_matters.advantage: Maxwell's equations are a high-yield unifying framework: many CSIR-NET problems reduce to choosing the right equation, symmetry and boundary condition before doing algebra.

gauss_electric.meaning: Electric charge is the source of electric-field divergence.

gauss_magnetic.meaning: There are no isolated magnetic monopoles in classical Maxwell theory; magnetic field lines have zero net flux through a closed surface.

faraday.meaning: A changing magnetic flux produces a circulating electric field.

ampere_maxwell.integral: ∮_C B·dl = μ₀ I_enclosed + μ₀ε₀ d/dt ∫_S E·dA
ampere_maxwell.meaning: Magnetic circulation is sourced by conduction current and displacement current.

mathematical_structure.integral_to_differential: Use Gauss's divergence theorem for flux integrals and Stokes' theorem for circulation integrals; compare the integrands for arbitrary volumes/surfaces.
mathematical_structure.symmetry_rule: Choose Gaussian surfaces or Amperian loops only when the field magnitude/direction is sufficiently symmetric. Symmetry is a justification, not a shortcut to be assumed.

derivations.title: Displacement current and charge conservation
derivations.goal: Show why Ampere's law requires the displacement-current term in a time-dependent situation.
steps: Start with the magnetostatic form ∇×B = μ₀J.
Take divergence of both sides: ∇·(∇×B)=0, so μ₀∇·J=0.
Charge conservation instead requires ∇·J = −∂ρ/∂t.
Using Gauss's law, ρ=ε₀∇·E, gives ∇·J = −ε₀∂(∇·E)/∂t.
Therefore the combination J+ε₀∂E/∂t has zero divergence.
The consistent local law is ∇×B=μ₀J+μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t.
The added term corresponds to displacement current density J_d=ε₀∂E/∂t.
derivations.exam_trap: Displacement current is not ordinary charge transport through the dielectric gap; it is the field term required by local charge conservation and produces magnetic circulation.

derivations.title: Electromagnetic wave equation in vacuum
derivations.goal: Derive the wave equation and propagation speed from the source-free Maxwell equations.
steps: In vacuum with ρ=0 and J=0, Gauss laws give ∇·E=0 and ∇·B=0.
Faraday's law gives ∇×E=−∂B/∂t.
Ampere-Maxwell law gives ∇×B=μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t.
Take curl of Faraday's law: ∇×(∇×E)=−∂(∇×B)/∂t.
Substitute the Ampere-Maxwell relation to obtain ∇²E=μ₀ε₀∂²E/∂t².
Similarly, ∇²B=μ₀ε₀∂²B/∂t².
Compare with the standard wave equation to obtain c=1/√(μ₀ε₀).
derivations.exam_trap: Do not insert ∇·E=0 in a material medium without checking whether free/bound charge and constitutive relations have been specified.

derivations.title: Poynting theorem and electromagnetic energy flow
derivations.goal: Derive the local electromagnetic energy balance from Maxwell's equations.
steps: Take E·(∇×H) and H·(∇×E) using ∇×H=J+∂D/∂t and ∇×E=−∂B/∂t.
Use the vector identity ∇·(E×H)=H·(∇×E)−E·(∇×H).
For a linear nondispersive medium with u=(E·D+B·H)/2, identify the time-derivative terms as ∂u/∂t.
Rearrange to obtain ∂u/∂t + ∇·S = −J·E.
Identify S=E×H as the Poynting vector and J·E as power delivered to charges per unit volume.
derivations.result: ∂u/∂t + ∇·S = −J·E, with S=E×H and u=(E·D+B·H)/2 for a linear nondispersive medium.
derivations.exam_trap: The Poynting vector gives energy flux density; its direction is not automatically the same as either E or B.

boundary_conditions: Tangential E continuity in the absence of singular time-varying magnetic flux: n×(E₂−E₁)=0.
Always define the interface normal and the direction of the cross product before applying signs.

electromagnetic_waves.plane_wave: For a uniform plane wave in a homogeneous source-free medium, E, B and the propagation direction k are mutually perpendicular.
relations: H=B/μ in a simple isotropic medium
electromagnetic_waves.polarization: The polarization is set by the direction and time dependence of E transverse to k; B follows from k×E/ω.

poynting.plane_wave: For a sinusoidal plane wave, the time-averaged intensity is ⟨S⟩=E₀²/(2η) for peak electric-field amplitude E₀.

worked_examples.title: Infinite line charge
worked_examples.problem: Find E at distance r from an infinite line charge density λ.
solution: Choose a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius r and length L.
Symmetry gives constant radial E on the curved surface and zero flux through the end caps.
Therefore E=λ/(2πε₀r) radial outward for λ>0.
worked_examples.trap: Do not use a spherical Gaussian surface for cylindrical symmetry.

worked_examples.title: Charging capacitor and displacement current
worked_examples.problem: A parallel-plate capacitor is charging with conduction current I. What displacement current crosses the gap in the ideal quasistatic limit?
solution: Ampere-Maxwell law must give the same magnetic circulation for a surface cutting the wire and a surface spanning the capacitor gap.
The changing electric flux satisfies ε₀ dΦ_E/dt=I for the ideal capacitor circuit.
worked_examples.trap: The equality is a circuit-level result for the ideal charging capacitor; it does not mean charge carriers cross the dielectric gap.

worked_examples.title: Vacuum wave speed
worked_examples.problem: Use μ₀ and ε₀ to determine the propagation speed of an electromagnetic wave in vacuum.
solution: The source-free wave equation has coefficient μ₀ε₀ multiplying the second time derivative.
This equals the vacuum speed of light c.
worked_examples.trap: The speed follows from the field equations; do not confuse it with material phase velocity 1/√(με).

worked_examples.title: Plane-wave energy flux
worked_examples.problem: A vacuum plane wave has peak electric-field amplitude E₀. Find its time-averaged Poynting magnitude.
solution: For a vacuum plane wave B₀=E₀/c and H₀=E₀/η₀.
The instantaneous flux is S=EH, and averaging sin² over a cycle gives 1/2.
worked_examples.trap: If E₀ is a peak amplitude, retain the factor 1/2; for RMS fields the expression changes accordingly.

practice_problems.question: Which Maxwell equation states that the net electric flux through a closed surface is proportional to enclosed charge?
practice_problems.explanation: Gauss's electric law relates closed-surface electric flux to enclosed charge.

practice_problems.explanation: The divergence theorem converts ∮E·dA into ∫∇·E dV.

practice_problems.question: In vacuum with no sources, the electric field satisfies:
practice_problems.explanation: Combining Faraday and Ampere-Maxwell laws gives the vacuum wave equation.

options: Perpendicular and both transverse to k
practice_problems.explanation: E, B and k form a mutually perpendicular triad.

practice_problems.question: The Poynting vector in a simple medium is:
practice_problems.explanation: Electromagnetic energy flux density is S=E×H.

practice_problems.explanation: Total flux depends only on enclosed charge, not Gaussian-surface radius.

practice_problems.explanation: The displacement current matches the conduction current in the ideal charging circuit.

practice_problems.question: At an interface carrying free surface current K, the tangential magnetic field obeys:
practice_problems.explanation: The boundary condition from Ampere's law is n×(H₂−H₁)=K_f.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using Gauss's law without sufficient symmetry.
common_mistakes.right: Use it for flux-source relations generally, but exploit constant-field simplifications only when symmetry justifies them.
common_mistakes.why: The integral law is always valid; the shortcut E A is not always valid.

common_mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the minus sign in Faraday's law.
common_mistakes.right: Keep −dΦ_B/dt and interpret it with Lenz's law.
common_mistakes.why: The sign encodes opposition to the change in magnetic flux.

common_mistakes.mistake: Treating displacement current as literal charge crossing the capacitor dielectric.
common_mistakes.right: It is ε₀∂E/∂t in vacuum and represents the field contribution to magnetic circulation.
common_mistakes.why: The term is required by continuity and produces the same Ampere circulation consistently.
There are no isolated magnetic monopoles in the theory.

common_mistakes.mistake: Dropping μ or ε in material-wave problems.
common_mistakes.right: Use v=1/√(με) and η=√(μ/ε) for a simple isotropic medium.

common_mistakes.mistake: Confusing E×H with E×B in a general medium.
common_mistakes.why: Energy flux is naturally expressed using E and H.

common_mistakes.mistake: Applying boundary conditions without defining the interface normal.
common_mistakes.right: State n from region 1 to region 2 before evaluating cross products.
common_mistakes.why: Most sign errors are orientation errors.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming E, B and k are parallel in an EM wave.
common_mistakes.right: For a plane wave in a simple homogeneous source-free medium they are mutually perpendicular.
common_mistakes.why: The curl equations enforce transverse fields.

common_mistakes.mistake: Using peak amplitude in an RMS intensity formula or vice versa.
common_mistakes.why: The factor 1/2 comes from time averaging a squared sinusoid.
Time-varying magnetic fields generate nonconservative electric fields.

connections: Electrostatics is recovered when ∂B/∂t=0 and charges are stationary.
Magnetostatics is recovered when ∂E/∂t=0 and currents are steady.
Electromagnetic waves emerge in source-free regions from the displacement-current term.
Boundary conditions connect Maxwell's local equations to interface problems.
Poynting's theorem turns Maxwell dynamics into an energy-conservation statement.

exam_patterns: Select the correct Maxwell equation from divergence/curl wording.
Use symmetry before evaluating a Gaussian flux or Ampere circulation.
Compare two Ampere surfaces in a charging capacitor.
Derive or identify the vacuum wave equation and speed.
Use interface boundary conditions with careful orientation.
Compute average Poynting flux from peak or RMS field amplitudes.
Check units, signs, source-free limits and static limits.
